newsitem.title: USA: Gulf War illness report due on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War illness report due on Tuesday.

text.p: A White House report scheduled for release on Tuesday is expected to criticise the Pentagon's investigation of Gulf War illness and recommend independent oversight of efforts to solve ailments affecting thousands of veterans of the 1991 war.

"I think you can safely assume it will be critical of the (Defense) Department. But not as critical as some people expect," one administration official familiar with the ongoing medical controversy told Reuters.

The official, who asked not to be identified, said the report to President Bill Clinton by a panel of scientists and defence experts supported Pentagon conclusions that there was no single "Gulf War Syndrome" and no common cause for the various complaints of veterans.

But an earlier draft of the special report by the Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans' Illnesses suggested in November that the Pentagon had lost credibility on the issue and outside investigators should take charge.
As many as 60,000 of the more than 500,000 U.S. troops who served in the Gulf have complained of ills ranging from memory loss to fatigue and muscle and joint pain.
Members of Congress and veterans groups have complained that the Pentagon investigation has been poorly handled.

The Pentagon says it has found no common cause for the complaints and no firm evidence that troops suffered from any exposure to Iraqi chemical or biological agents during the war, in which a U.S.-led military coalition drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait.

The Pentagon also says there is no evidence that Iraq even used chemical arms in the war, but it announced last year that as many as 20,000 U.S. troops might have been been exposed to nerve agents in the March 1991 destruction of an Iraqi artillery dump.

That destruction of ammunition by U.S. military engineers at Kamisiyah in southern Iraq sent up a giant blast cloud, and the Pentagon is now investigating whether U.S. soldiers suffered low-level exposure from fallout.

Some members of Congress and veterans groups, noting that the Kamisiyah incident was not revealed until last year, have accused the department of bumbling and even outright cover-up of Gulf War illness.
An ongoing CIA analysis of wind and other weather patterns in the area at the time has so far been inconclusive.

The Pentagon, which has sponsored a number of studies of Gulf War illness, last month launched a new $2.5 million effort that will include a close look at the effects of low-level exposure to chemical agents.

But defence analysts say they expect the controversy over complaints from Gulf War troops, which is also ongoing in Britain, to continue for years because of the difficulty of determining whether chemicals, pesticides, pollution or a mixture of any of those could cause lasting ill-effects.
